raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male patient was referred to our tertiary hospital with complaints of worsening abdominal swelling over the past 2 weeks, a condition that began in childhood. He reported a history of intermittent abdominal cramps, shortness of breath, and early satiety. Since the age of 12, he had experienced repeated admissions to a primary hospital and had undergone peritoneal tapping twice per month, attributed to suspected ascites secondary to chronic liver disease. He also reported difficulty lying supine.
On examination, the patient appeared chronically ill. His vital signs were in normal range except for tachypnea of 48 breaths per minute. Chest examination revealed decreased air entry over the lower posterior one-third of the right lung field. Abdominal examination revealed a grossly distended abdomen (Fig. 1) with a palpable, firm, and non-tender mass measuring 20 x 30 cm.
Laboratory analysis revealed an alkaline phosphatase level elevated to five times the normal limit. Other blood test results were within normal ranges.
An abdominal ultrasound revealed a large multicystic intra-abdominal mass with peripheral calcification, displacing the liver superiorly as well as the spleen and bowel loops anterolaterally. Additionally, another hypoechoic mass measuring 2 x 1.5 cm with peripheral enhancement was identified in segment VI of the liver.
An abdominal CT scan demonstrated a massive non-enhancing cystic mass with a thick rim of peripheral calcification, measuring 21 x 28 cm, containing peripherally located daughter cysts and pushing the gallbladder anteriorly. Another well-defined, thin-walled, large peritoneal cystic mass, and measuring 13 x 24 x 28 cm, was observed. This mass exhibited fluid attenuation and a focal anteroposterior wall defect, closely apposed to the hepatic cystic mass. It displaced bowel loops, great vessels, and the right kidney posteroinferiorly while mediating the pancreas.
Further findings included pericalyceal dilatation of the right kidney with an atrophied and thinned-out cortex. Additionally, there was a fluid-attenuating collection measuring ~2.3 cm in depth within the right pleural cavity (Fig. 2).
The surgical operation was planned as a semi-elective laparotomy. A midline incision was made, revealing a 25 x 25 cm cystic mass with a calcified wall located at segments IVB, V, and VII of the liver, pushing against and attached to the gallbladder. This mass communicated with another peritoneal cystic mass measuring 20 x 20 cm, containing 20 liters of fluid and hydatid sand, and displacing the entire bowel to the left (Figs 3 and 4). Segment VI of the liver was thinned out and contained two additional active cysts. The right kidney was atrophied and displayed a 'water bag' appearance. The peritoneal surface and diaphragm were calcified, and adhesions were observed between the intra-abdominal cyst, abdominal wall, and urinary bladder. About 96% alcohol was used as a sclerosing agent.
A total pericystectomy, cholecystectomy, and segmental resection of segment VI with the active cysts were performed. A drain was placed in the peritoneal cavity.
Intraoperatively, the patient developed shock, requiring the initiation, and gradual escalation of a low dose of noradrenaline. Postoperatively, he was transferred to the surgical intensive care unit for further management. Within 24 hours, his shock resolved, noradrenaline was tapered and discontinued, and he underwent a pleural tap, yielding 400 ml of serous fluid with non-revealing pleural fluid analysis. The chest condition subsequently improved, and the patient was extubated. By the fourth postoperative day, he was transferred to the recovery unit.
Postoperative albendazole therapy was initiated for a planned duration of six months. The patient was discharged from the hospital 10 days after surgery. He returned to the surgical referral clinic a week later, where the drain was removed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with worsening abdominal swelling over the past 2 weeks on a background of chronic abdominal distension since childhood.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had progressive abdominal distension beginning in childhood, accompanied by intermittent abdominal cramps, shortness of breath, early satiety, and orthopnea (difficulty lying supine). Since age 12, he had been repeatedly admitted to a primary hospital and subjected to twice-monthly peritoneal paracenteses for presumed ascites secondary to chronic liver disease, before presenting with acute worsening over 2 weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of childhood-onset abdominal distension treated with repeated therapeutic paracenteses twice monthly since age 12 for misdiagnosed cirrhotic ascites.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe abdominal swelling, intermittent abdominal cramps, dyspnea, orthopnea, and early satiety.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically ill-appearing male with tachypnea (respiratory rate 48 breaths/min) and otherwise normal vital signs. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry over the lower posterior one-third of the right lung field. Abdominal exam showed gross distension with a firm, non-tender palpable mass measuring 20 x 30 cm.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase was elevated to 5 times the upper limit of normal; other blood tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed a massive multicystic intra-abdominal mass with peripheral calcification displacing the liver, spleen, and bowel loops, plus a 2 x 1.5 cm hypoechoic lesion in hepatic segment VI.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominopelvic CT demonstrated a massive 21 x 28 cm non-enhancing hepatic cystic mass with thick peripheral calcification and peripheral daughter cysts in segments IVB, V, and VII communicating through a focal wall defect with a 13 x 24 x 28 cm peritoneal cyst displacing the bowel, great vessels, and right kidney (which showed severe hydronephrotic cortical atrophy), alongside two active cysts in segment VI and a 2.3-cm right pleural effusion. Midline laparotomy evacuated 20 liters of fluid and hydatid sand using 96% alcohol sclerotherapy, with total pericystectomy, cholecystectomy, and segment VI resection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Giant ruptured hepatic hydatid cyst (25 x 25 cm in segments IVB, V, VII) communicating with a 20-liter secondary peritoneal hydatid cyst and two active segment VI cysts, complicated by right renal pressure atrophy and reactive right pleural effusion. Following total pericystectomy, cholecystectomy, segment VI resection, and 96% alcohol sclerotherapy, transient intraoperative/ICU shock was managed with low-dose noradrenaline and a 400-mL serous thoracentesis; he was extubated within 24 hours, discharged on postoperative day 10 on a 6-month course of oral albendazole, and had his peritoneal drain removed 1 week later.
